explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. God says, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” He tells them who He is and what He's done before He says a single command. Introductions first, instructions second. I like that order.

Close, but the Jordan doesn't come up here. What God says is that He brought them “…out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” The people are at the mountain while He speaks (Exodus 19:2). So the rescue He points to is the one behind them.

Canaan isn't in this opening line, friend. God points backward, to the One who “…brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” That's the introduction He chooses. Before He talks about anywhere new, He names what He has already done.

explanations.answer: Have no other gods before Him
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. God says, “You shall have no other gods before Me.” No second place, no backup, no spare one tucked in the cupboard. It's the very first command out of His mouth.

explanations.answer: Build Him an altar on the mountain
explanations.explanation: No altar in this first command, friend. God says, “You shall have no other gods before Me.” That's where the commands begin. Nothing here asks for building anything yet.

explanations.answer: Bring Him an offering each morning
explanations.explanation: I get why a morning offering sounds right, friend. It sounds like something a good baker would do before the oven's even warm. But it's not in these verses. God opens with “You shall have no other gods before Me.” (Exodus 20:3). Before anything else, He wants to be the only God on the list.

explanations.answer: An idol of anything in heaven or earth
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. God says, “You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in the heavens above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath.” Sky, land, sea, He covers all three. Nothing is left out, so there's no loophole to hunt for.

explanations.answer: A tower that reaches up to heaven
explanations.explanation: No towers in this command, friend. God says not to make “…an idol in the form of anything in the heavens above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath.” The command is about idols. Building up toward heaven isn't mentioned here.

explanations.answer: A king like all the other nations
explanations.explanation: A king is a big thing to want, friend, but this command isn't about thrones. God says, “You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in the heavens above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath.” (Exodus 20:4). Sky, land and sea, and not one of them gets made into an idol. The command is about idols, and a king doesn't show up in it.

You've got it, baker! God says, “for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God…” (Exodus 20:5). He says it right after telling them not to bow down to idols or worship them. He doesn't want to share the spot. Nice and clean, just like a good stamp.

Patient is a word I'd love to bake with, but it's not the word here. The verse says, “for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God…” That's how God describes Himself in this moment. He's talking about idols, and He uses that word.

Silent can't be it, friend, because God is talking the whole time. The passage opens with “And God spoke all these words…” (Exodus 20:1). The word He uses for Himself here is “jealous.” Silent would be a pretty quiet mountain, and this one is thundering.

True, baker. God speaks of “…showing loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments.” Look at the numbers. Just before that, He says “…the third and fourth generations…” for those who hate Him. A thousand is a LOT more than four.

It's actually true, friend. God speaks of “…showing loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments.” Put that next to the “…third and fourth generations…” He mentions just before. A thousand generations is a much bigger number, and I'd rather count that batch.

It's the other way around, friend. God says, “…for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain.” He doesn't say He'll let it go. So the answer is False, and the text is plain about it.
That's right. God says, “…for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain.” So the statement on the card has it backward. It's a serious line, and God means it.
Yes, the seventh day. God says, “…but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God…” Six days for labor, then the seventh belongs to the LORD. Count it on your fingers if you need to.
That's the word. On the Sabbath, God says, “…you must not do any work…” Six days to labor, then the seventh is set aside from it. For one whole day, the to-do list gets put down.

The first day is actually one of the working days. God says, “Six days you shall labor and do all your work…” and the Sabbath comes after those. The day He names is the seventh. So the first day falls with the labor.
Travel isn't the word here, friend. God says the seventh day is a Sabbath on which “…you must not do any work…” He doesn't mention travel in these verses. Work is the word on the page.

There's no eighth day in this command. God says, “Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God.” Six plus the seventh makes the week. An eighth day would be a bonus nobody was handed.

True, baker. God says that on the Sabbath you must not do any work, “…neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your manservant or maidservant or livestock…” The livestock is right there in the list. Even the animals get the day.

It's True, friend. The list reads “…neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your manservant or maidservant or livestock…” The livestock is named right in the middle of it. Somebody go tell the animals.

explanations.answer: He made everything in six days and rested on the seventh
explanations.explanation: You nailed it, friend. God says, “For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested.” That's the reason He gives for the Sabbath. It points all the way back to creation.

explanations.answer: Israel rested for seven days after leaving Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason God gives here. He says, “For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested.” His reason is about what He did at creation. Nothing in this passage mentions a seven day rest after Egypt.

explanations.answer: Moses waited seven days at the foot of the mountain
explanations.explanation: Moses is Israel's leader, but his waiting isn't the reason here. God says, “For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested.” The reason comes from what God did. It has nothing to do with a wait at the mountain.

explanations.answer: So their days may be long in the land
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. God says, “Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.” This command comes with its reason attached. And the land is something the LORD is giving.

explanations.answer: So their father's land will pass to them
explanations.explanation: Nothing about land passing down in this verse, friend. God says, “Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.” The land is the one the LORD is giving. The reason is long days there.

explanations.answer: So their own children will honor them
explanations.explanation: That one sounds sweet, friend, like a family love loop. But the verse gives a different reason. God says, “Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.” The reason attached is long days in that land. It's about the one honoring, and about a land the LORD is giving.

Look again, friend. The Sabbath comes with a reason in verse 11, and honoring parents comes with one in verse 12. But these four are short and sweet: “You shall not murder.” “You shall not commit adultery.” “You shall not steal.” “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.” No reason follows any of them, so the answer is False.

Right. The Sabbath comes with a reason in verse 11, and honoring parents comes with one in verse 12. But these four stand alone: “You shall not murder.” “You shall not commit adultery.” “You shall not steal.” “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.” God just says them, short and plain.

You got it, baker. God says, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house.” and the list ends with “…anything that belongs to your neighbor.” Wanting what's on the neighbor's side of the fence is the thing He names. Eyes on your own cookie tray, friend.

A master isn't named in this command. God says, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house.” and ends with “…anything that belongs to your neighbor.” The one whose things these are is the neighbor. That's the word God uses.

The text never says enemy here. God says, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house.” and ends with “…anything that belongs to your neighbor.” The word He uses is neighbor, and that's the one to hold onto.

Not quite, friend. The text says, “…they trembled and stood at a distance.” (Exodus 20:18). Thunder, lightning, a ram's horn and a mountain wrapped in smoke, and the people stay at a distance. They don't rush closer. If my kitchen did all that, I'd be standing by the door too. So the answer is False.
Right. The text says, “…they trembled and stood at a distance.” Nobody rushes closer to the thunder and the smoke. Honestly, I can't picture it going any other way.

explanations.answer: That Moses speak to them instead of God
explanations.explanation: That's what they ask. They tell Moses, Israel's leader, “Speak to us yourself and we will listen…” Then they add, “But do not let God speak to us, or we will die.” They want Moses between them and God's voice.

explanations.answer: That Moses take them back to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt doesn't come up in what they say. They tell Moses, Israel's leader, “Speak to us yourself and we will listen…” Then they add, “But do not let God speak to us, or we will die.” Their request is about who does the speaking.

explanations.answer: That Moses lead them away from Sinai
explanations.explanation: They don't ask to leave the mountain. They tell Moses, Israel's leader, “Speak to us yourself and we will listen…” Then they add, “But do not let God speak to us, or we will die.” They ask Moses to speak instead of God.

True, baker. Moses, Israel's leader, replies, “Do not be afraid…” The people had just said they might die if God spoke to them, so Moses has something to answer. He then tells them, “For God has come to test you, so that the fear of Him may be before you, to keep you from sinning.”

It's actually True, friend. Moses, Israel's leader, replies, “Do not be afraid…” He follows it with, “For God has come to test you, so that the fear of Him may be before you, to keep you from sinning.” Those are his words to the trembling people.

That's the word. Moses, Israel's leader, says God has come to test them, “…so that the fear of Him may be before you, to keep you from sinning.” Staying out of sin is the goal he names. It's Moses' own explanation.

Fleeing isn't the word, friend, even if standing at a distance feels close to it. Moses, Israel's leader, says the fear of God is “…to keep you from sinning.” Sinning is what the fear is meant to keep them from.

Fighting isn't in Moses' words. Moses, Israel's leader, says God has come to test them, “…so that the fear of Him may be before you, to keep you from sinning.” The word he uses is sinning. No fists involved.

Not quite, friend. The people do stand at a distance, but Moses doesn't stay with them. The text says, “…the people stood at a distance as Moses approached the thick darkness where God was.” So the answer is False.

Right. The people stood at a distance, but Moses, Israel's leader, “…approached the thick darkness where God was.” Everybody else is holding their ground and he's walking toward it. That's the picture the verse gives.
